question: EU animal welfare provisions and laws reflect, inter alia, what are termed the five freedoms: (1) freedom from hunger or thirst, (2) freedom from discomfort, (3) freedom from pain, injury or disease, (4) freedom to express normal behaviour, and (5) freedom from fear and distress.

For many years, however, Spanish authorities have accepted that hunting dogs can inter alia be hanged from trees, doused with acid or chained to moving cars in order to see which animal is best suited for hunting. These atrocities, and many others, are tolerated and go unpunished despite clearly violating numerous EU animal welfare provisions and laws.
More than 50 000 hunting dogs, including breeds such as Galgos and Podencos, fall victim to this cruel and disgusting ‘tradition’ every year. 1.
How is it possible for an EU Member State to violate EU animal welfare provisions and not be penalised?
Are the Spanish authorities allowed to explicitly exclude Spanish hunting and working dogs from the scope of animal welfare laws?

Why is the Commission turning a blind eye and not analysing why, for more than nine years, protest marches by more and more people, accompanied by extensive media coverage, have been taking place in more and more cities in Europe, and beyond, in support of Spanish hunting dogs and against Spain’s animal welfare law?
answer: The Commission condemns any form of cruelty towards animals in line with Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (1) where animals are recognised as sentient beings.

Whereas the EU has adopted animal welfare legislation covering slaughter (Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009) (2), in the case of animals kept for farming purposes (Directive 98/58/EC) (3) and on the protection of animals during transport (Regulation (EC) No 1/2005) (4), it has no competence to legislate on the welfare of all animals, such as hunting dogs, generally.

The Commission has recently adopted a proposal for a regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceabilit y (5), which is currently before the co-legislators. Under the proposed rules, any natural or legal person who keeps more than three bitches which in total produce two litters or more per calendar year, would be subject to specific animal welfare requirements for breeding establishments.

The proposed rules would therefore cover hunters who meet the above-mentioned criteria, in which case they would have to comply with detailed obligations to protect the welfare of breeding dogs and their offspring.
